stories.headline: Man arrested in killings of three elderly men in Puna
stories.summary: Hawaiʻi Island police arrested 36-year-old Jacob Jake Daniel Baker, found hiding in a small cave after a manhunt, in connection with three killings in Puna.
stories.text: Hawaiʻi Island police have arrested 36-year-old Pāhoa resident Jacob Jake Daniel Baker in connection with the killings of three elderly men in Puna. Authorities say Baker was found hiding in a small cave Thursday after an island-wide manhunt. The victims include Robert Shine, 69, who was found partially submerged in a cement pond and died from strangulation. 69-year-old John Kars, who died from sharp force trauma, and a 79-year-old man, believed by friends to be Chita Morse, who suffered apparent blunt force injuries.

stories.headline: UH survey seeks ways to control invasive fruit flies
stories.summary: UH tropical agriculture researchers are surveying farmers, gardeners and landscapers on controlling invasive fruit flies, with field studies on four islands.
stories.text: What about fruit flies? People who study tropical agriculture at UH are conducting a survey asking farmers, home gardeners, and landscapers to find out how to control those annoying, invasive fruit flies. Field studies are happening on Hawaiʻi Island, Kauai, Maui, and Oahu, including baiting techniques to trap the little buggers.

stories.headline: Lahaina Homecoming invites former residents back in July
stories.summary: The inaugural three-day Lahaina Homecoming runs July 17 through 19, with a competition offering round-trip flights for up to 80 former Lahaina residents.
stories.text: Lahaina families and community members are invited to return home for the inaugural Lahaina Homecoming, a three-day gathering focused on healing, reconnection, and rebuilding, taking place July 17 through 19, 2026. Organizers have also launched the E Hoʻi Mai competition, offering round-trip flights from the continental U.S. for up to 80 former Lahaina residents To return home for the weekend. Applicants are asked to submit a short video sharing their family's connection to Lahaina and hopes for its future. More information and applications are available through the Lahaina Homecoming website.

stories.text: It has been widely reported that addiction to social media is harmful to children and several countries are restricting the use of cell phones by young adults. Now new cell Phone limits are coming for Hawaiʻi students beginning this fall. A new statewide policy will prohibit elementary and middle school students from using cell phones during school hours. High school students will not be able to use them during instructional time. Some teachers, however, are skeptical, saying that some kids are going to figure out how to get around the restrictions like they always do.

stories.headline: Film industry panel on Maui's creative economy set for Saturday
stories.summary: Film leaders will hold a free panel at the MEDB Malcolm Center in Kīhei on May 30 on moving Maui County from a film industry to a film economy.
stories.text: Maui's Film Industry Leaders will gather tomorrow, Saturday, May 30th. The show will be broadcast on the 20th from noon to 2 p.m. at the MEDB Malcolm Center in Kīhei for a panel discussion titled Infrastructure of Stories, Moving Maui County from Film Industry to Film Economy. Panelists include Emmy-winning Shogun executive producer Rachel Kondo, Maui film commissioner Brian Kohn, filmmaker Matt Yamashita, showrunner Kavika Hoke, and director-writer Stefan Schaeffer. The free event will explore strategies for growing Maui's creative economy through film and storytelling. The MEDB Malcolm Center is located at 1305 North Holopono Street, Suite 5, and advance registration is requested.

stories.summary: The Hawaii Journalism Initiative reports many Kīhei road sinkholes need repairs with no clear cost or timetable, and South Kīhei Road is hit hardest.

stories.headline: Basil is Hawaii's number one herb crop
stories.summary: Hawaii exports millions of pounds of basil to Canada and the U.S. mainland, and the industry is worth nearly 43 billion dollars.
stories.text: Hawaiʻi grows a lot of herb, but the number one crop is not what you're thinking. It's basil. The Aloha State exports millions of pounds to Canada and the U.S. mainland, and the industry here is worth nearly $43 billion dollars, three times larger than that of bananas Basil is just behind algae, coffee, cattle, and seed crops on the list of Hawaiʻi's most lucrative crops.

stories.headline: Two Kahului residents named Maui's outstanding older Americans
stories.summary: The Office on Aging honored Joseph Pontinella and Roselani Enomoto for leadership and lifelong service, along with 11 other nominees.
stories.text: Every year, the Maui Department of Human Concern's Office on Aging picks a male and female outstanding older American, and they get a plaque to put on their wall. stories.headline: Commission on Children and Youth weighs independent youth advisory group
stories.summary: The commission discussed a youth-led advisory group and heard testimony from Spirit Horse Ranch about its equine therapy sessions and funding challenges.
stories.text: Let's give the kids a chance to speak up and to speak out. The Maui County Commission on Children and Youth discussed forming a new independent youth advisory group to give Maui youth a stronger voice in county issues and policy discussions. The group would remain youth-led and independent from county authority. The Commission also heard emotional testimony from Spirit Horse Ranch, which says it's provided more than 5,000 trauma-informed equine therapy sessions to Maui youth and families since the line of fires, even as the ranch struggles with funding challenges.

stories.headline: Returning to Makaluapuna Point and Dragon's Teeth
stories.summary: A feature visits Makaluapuna Point in Kapalua, where hardened lava formations known as Dragon's Teeth reflect the island's geological history.
stories.text: Macaluapuna Point has always been a favorite place on Maui. We come back here often because it's one of those places where you can clearly see how the island itself was formed. The trail crosses hardened lava fields created by volcanic activity thousands of years ago. This area is also known as Dragon's Teeth and once you stand here, it's easy to understand why. The lava rock rises from the ground in sharp black points. They look like giant teeth Coming out of the earth, some are narrow and jagged, others curved and uneven, shaped by molten lava cooling quickly against the ocean and then carved over time by wind, salt and And erosion. What we see today is a reminder that the Hawaiian islands were built by eruptions from the seafloor Of a million of years. Walking here, we are literally standing on the geological history of Maui. Places like These are approached with respect, not just as scenic location, but as part of a larger relationship between nature, history, and community.

stories.headline: Tulsi Gabbard resigns as Director of National Intelligence

stories.text: Former Hawaiʻi Congresswoman Tulsi Gabbard is out as Director of National Intelligence and has resigned her position effective June 30th. She said the reason she is stepping down is to look after her husband who is being diagnosed with a rare form of bone cancer. In a letter to President Trump, she expressed her gratitude for the opportunity to serve. stories.text: So we went from 11 hives to 44, to 88, to 160 and we're up to around 300 now. So this is how we extract the honey. We'll bring in a thousand pounds or so from the bee yards. And the frames are individually uncapped. This is an uncapping machine. And Dusty's going to show you. So the uncapper takes off most of it. Sometimes it misses some, like on the backside, and then that has to be hand done by Sarah. And after the cappings are removed, the frame can go in the extractor. We put 20 frames in each extractor, and then centrifugal force throws the honey out of the frame. Once the frames are empty, they get stacked up and put back on the bees and the bees rob them all out so there's no loss, no waste. And once the honey is collected, it's pumped across the ceiling into these storage tanks where we allow the wax to float to the surface. We don't use any heat to separate wax and honey. It's a cold process. This is the bottling machine. This is a proportioner which puts the same amount of honey in every jar. It's important to note that we don't use any heat in this process because heat destroys the enzymes that the bees put into the honey to make it honey. And after the honey is bottled, then we label it and put it into a cool storage area. Temperature controlled. We hold it at about 58 degrees. And when we're done harvesting, this room is completely full. Sealing to floor. We harvest about 25,000 pounds per year.
